title: Professional teeth cleaning: advantages and disadvantages
intro: Professional teeth cleaning removes plaque and tartar that brushing cannot reach, and is often offered as part of dental care. It can leave teeth feeling smooth and fresh. Evidence for long-term benefits for healthy people is limited, so the question is whom it helps most and how often it is needed.

sections.heading: What it involves
paragraphs: A dental professional uses hand instruments, ultrasonic scalers and polishing tools to remove hard deposits called tartar or calculus and soft plaque from above and just below the gum line. Teeth are then polished and fluoride may be applied. The procedure takes about thirty to sixty minutes and is done at a dental practice.

sections.heading: Possible advantages
paragraphs: Removing tartar helps control gum inflammation and may reduce gum bleeding and bad breath. For people with gum disease, professional cleaning is part of effective treatment. It gives an opportunity to receive advice on cleaning technique, and to detect problems early. Many people like the clean feeling and the cosmetic effect of stain removal.

sections.heading: Possible disadvantages
paragraphs: Some people experience temporary sensitivity or gum soreness. Aggressive cleaning can remove tooth substance or irritate gums. For people without gum disease, studies have not shown clear long-term benefits for preventing decay or tooth loss beyond good home care. It can be costly, because in many places insurance does not cover routine cleaning beyond tartar removal.

sections.heading: Who benefits most
paragraphs: People with gum disease or a tendency to quickly build up tartar, those with braces, implants or dentures, people with difficulty cleaning because of disability, and smokers may benefit more. Frequency should be tailored to risk, from once or twice a year to every three months for those with gum disease.

sections.heading: Home care remains key
paragraphs: Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between the teeth daily, limiting sugary food and drink and not smoking matter most. Ask your dentist what a cleaning will involve, how often you need it, what it costs and whether part of it is covered by your insurance.

examples.title: Asking about frequency
examples.text: Imagine your practice offers cleaning every six months. You could ask whether this interval suits your risk, and what the dentist found at your last visit.

examples.title: Comparing costs
examples.text: Suppose you want a cleaning but your insurer pays only for tartar removal. You might ask what is included and what extra charges apply.

questions: How often do I need professional cleaning, given my risk?
What will it cost, and what does insurance cover?
How can I improve my home care?
